---
title: "Derive a scenario from data"
---

*Simulate ▸ Derive scenario* turns a real dataset into a scenario that simulates
studies like it: the plasmode idea, without sharing the data.

![Derive scenario on a cohort: variables, conditional effects with the round-trip check, latent correlations.](screenshots/s12-derive.png){.screenshot}

## What it estimates

- the **marginal** distribution of each variable (normal, log-normal, gamma or
  uniform; Poisson or negative binomial for counts; category proportions);
- the **latent correlations**, by inverting the Gaussian copula the simulator
  uses, so a simulated study reproduces the observed correlations;
- the **conditional effects** on the outcome (logistic, linear, Poisson or Cox,
  with 95% CI and the crude estimate), and the prevalence, mean, risk or Weibull
  shape that calibrates it.

*Check by simulating* analyses one large study simulated from the derived scenario
with the same model: the **Re-estimated** column should match the adjusted
estimates.

![The round-trip check.](screenshots/s13-derive-effects.png){.screenshot width=85%}

### Missing values

*Missing values in the variables* chooses how the outcome model deals with rows
that miss a covariate (the distributions and correlations always use every
observed value, and the outcome targets every row with the outcome):

| method | cost | what it gives |
|---|---|---|
| Complete cases | none | unbiased when missingness does not depend on the outcome; loses rows |
| Mean / most frequent value | none | keeps every row, but dilutes the associations and understates the uncertainty |
| Single imputation | low | chained equations (each variable from the others and the outcome, with its noise): unbiased under missing at random, intervals too narrow |
| Multiple imputation | m times higher | m sets, each model on a bootstrap sample, pooled by Rubin's rules: the reference method |

With an imputation method the table also shows the complete-case estimate.
*Derive* also warns when few rows are complete, when a variable is missing
mostly in one outcome group (probably recorded after the outcome), when there are
fewer than 10 events per coefficient (with a shrinkage factor), when an effect is
not estimable, and when times look like days or months.

### Values that do not apply

Real datasets record some variables only for some people: the age at first
oral contraceptive use is blank for women who never used them, the years of use
are 0, the age at the first smear test is coded 99 when there was none. Before
estimating anything, *Derive*:

- reads an all-nines value at the top of a variable's range (99, 999), far more
  frequent than the values just below it, as **missing**;
- finds variables that are missing, or one constant, in a level of another
  variable and observed elsewhere (**structural values**). The scenario writes
  them with `only_if`/`otherwise` (e.g. `only_if: co == "sí"`, `otherwise: 0`),
  their distribution comes from the people they apply to, their correlations
  with that variable are left out (it is a rule), and the model gives the other
  rows the `otherwise` value, so no rows are lost: the effect of the variable is
  among those it applies to, and the effect of the other variable is at the
  `otherwise` value;
- reports pairs of numbers whose order the data never break (start age ≤ end
  age ≤ age): the scenario cannot keep such an order, so write one from the
  other with a `formula` or leave one out.

Columns that jamovi read as nominal but hold numbers (integers from a CSV) are
read as numbers. Try it with
[chd_sim.csv](screenshots/chd_sim.csv), a simulated cohort.

## Finishing it with an AI

The data cannot tell causes from correlates, so a derived scenario has undirected
correlations and raw column names. *Export scenario* writes it as YAML with a
`derivation:` block (source, original names, missing data, estimates and
correlations), which is what an AI needs to finish it:

- [**A prompt for any AI**](https://github.com/victor-moreno/jamovi-studysim/blob/main/ai/prompt-derive-to-scenario.md):
  attach the exported YAML and `schema.md`. It returns the scenario with names and
  translations, a causal structure, rules for impossible combinations, rounded
  effects, a teaching note and references marked *to verify*, plus a report of
  its decisions.
- [**A Claude skill**](https://github.com/victor-moreno/jamovi-studysim/tree/main/ai/studysim-scenario)
  (also as a zip in the Releases): the same steps, with a validator,
  `check_scenario.R`, that checks the file, simulates a large study and compares
  the re-estimated effects with the data's, following renamed variables and
  changed reference categories.

Review the result before teaching with it: the causal structure is a judgement,
and references must be checked.
